name: Trados Nose-Shaper (Trilety)

card.summary: An early 1900s harness-style nose device sold as a painless way to reshape the nose through steady pressure, worn mostly at night.
card.note: Historical device; no published trials of nose-shaping harnesses exist.

quick.overview:
The Trados nose-shaper, sold by Trilety, belongs to a class of early 20th-century mechanical nose correctors. These were metal and fabric devices strapped over the nose to reshape it at home, as a non-surgical route to a straighter or finer nose.

A comparable 1907 US patent describes a bendable metal shaper with a soft lining, held on by straps over the forehead and behind the neck, worn at night, and described by its inventor as painless.
quick.how: Devices of this type were worn for periods, typically at night, with gentle continuous pressure from a lined metal piece and straps, adjusted for one-sided noses.
quick.risks: No published studies have tested such harnesses. Modern surgeons describe nasal cartilage and bone changes as generally requiring surgery; such devices are of historical interest.

lead: The Trados nose-shaper, marketed under the Trilety name as Model 22 or 25, belongs to a class of early-1900s mechanical devices sold for reshaping the nose at home.

A US patent of the same type, number 850,978, granted on 23 April 1907 to Ignatius Nathaniel Soares of Framingham, Massachusetts, describes the design: a thin tempered metal body that can be bent, a soft lining, and a tongue under the nose that presses the cartilage, held by buckled bands behind the neck and over the forehead.[1] The inventor describes it as producing a light steady tension, usually worn at night, and as painless; it could be adjusted more on one side for a one-sided nose.[1] The patent is cited here for the device class, and it is not identified as the Trados model.

chain: Lined metal piece rests on the nose
Straps hold gentle steady pressure, usually at night
Claimed gradual reshaping of the nose
angle.text: Sellers presented it as a painless, at-home way to straighten or refine the nose through steady pressure. No studies have tested it.

paras: The 1907 patent describes a bendable tempered-metal body lined with chamois or fabric, a projecting tongue resting under the nose, and two buckled bands crossing behind the neck and fastening over the forehead.[1] It was intended for upturned, one-sided or flat noses and distended nostrils.[1]

timeline.event: US patent 850,978 for a comparable strap-on nose-shaper granted.[1]
